why: German's adjective is silbern; bare *silber* is attributive colloquial at best, which is why every example on the card used the noun instead. Re-termed rather than re-posed: the card is about the colour word, and the colour word is silbern.
Same as silber: the adjective is golden. «Die Uhr glänzt gold» is colloquial and the card's other example was the noun.

normal is both, but carding it as an adverb costs a real capability: only adjective cards get de-inflection, so «ein normaler Tag» resolved to nothing and an example written that way was refused by the authoring gate. As an adjective it still reads adverbially — German adverbs are uninflected adjectives.
Adjective plus noun with no article, so it failed every noun rule and was the one articleless card outside Countries. It is a phrase and is now carded as one.

A southern German and Austrian regionalism sitting at A1, where it competed for the surface form with the A1 adverb *früh* that every beginner needs. The word is not hard, it is marked — B1 is where a learner meets a regional variant knowingly.
A shoemaker's last at A2. The word survives mainly in one idiom («Schuster, bleib bei deinem Leisten»), which is C1 territory, not second-semester vocabulary.

The noun *die Tausend* held the A1 slot for *thousand* while the numeral tausend — which is what an A1 learner needs, and what `hundert` already is — could not be authored, because this card claimed the surface form. Moved to B1 so the numeral can take A1.
